items.title: Show HN: Self-bench – benchmark coding agents on real-world software
items.summary: Hey HN, Today, we're launching selfbench.dev, an open-source tool that lets you create and run evals automatically from your PRs. Every benchmark with sufficient trust eventually gets benchmaxxed (Goodhart's law) - the labs are incentivized to maximize their scores on that benchmark, which isn't predictive on whether it'll actually work within your setup. This has been a time-consuming process that only the largest companies can afford to do, so we built self-bench to fix this. Self-bench uses agents to author / review Harbor environments generated from your PRs. You then approve every eval that the agent created, and can model/harness evals concurrently on sandboxes. To save you money, we also allow you to connect your OpenAI and Claude subscriptions so you don't have to pay raw token costs. We ran evals on several large codebases like - Posthog ( https://selfbench.dev/PostHog/posthog ) - Next.js ( https://selfbench.dev/vercel/next.js ) - Sentry ( https://selfbench.dev/getsentry/sentry ) - Pi ( https://selfbench.dev/earendil-works/pi ) - as well as other fantastic open-source projects (all on selfbench.dev) From our evals: - Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3 are almost always more expensive, yet less performant than models like GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, due to token efficiency. - GPT-6 Luna is almost always the most effective "cost-efficient" model we've tested, not open-source models. We'd love for you to try this on your codebase and let us know what you think!

items.title: Show HN: Open-Source Instinct
items.summary: We’ve all heard that Instinct raised $1 billion to bring personal AI agents to everyone. But I think anyone can build their own Instinct for a specific group of people. You know your audience, understand what they need, and know how to reach them. So I built an open-source version. It can make purchases online, coordinate with other people’s agents, use a computer, connect to MCP tools, manage permissions + everything else instinct wants to do. Here’s the stack: - Pi, the open-source agent framework used by openclaw - Maritime for each agent’s VM and computer access (cheapest infra) - Composio for app integrations and managed Google OAuth - Inkbox for imessege + email If you want to start selling your own personal AI agent, you can host the backend on a platform like railway/vercel (around $20 a month). Maritime handles provisioning each agent’s VM and the infrastructure behind it ($1 a month per agent) I’m open-sourcing this so we can build on it together: add more services and tools, better permissions, different payment strategies, better prompts... The goal is to make it easy and affordable for anyone to launch a startup selling agents so that the world isnt ruled by openai dots and meta muses Check it out and let me know what you think!

items.title: Show HN: Abralo - Open source Slack for agents and people
items.summary: Hi guys, Posted this ( https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48832797 ) on HN a few months ago when it was a different product (and closed source). It was originally a way of managing multiple agents in parallel (like TMUX, but with a nicer chat UI). But I found that I was only able to work with 3 or 4 agents simultaneously without information overload, so I decided to morph it into something which resembles Slack, where you can either privately speak to agents or address a room (like a channel) full of them. Importantly though, the agents can delegate work to each other, create other agents etc. Also had lots of user feedback from the first launch which means we've added multiple harnesses (Codex, OpenCode and waiting for Anthropic to approve Claude Code), git worktrees, connections to hundreds of MCPs, CLIs and APIs, browser-use and a proactive Chief of Staff (which periodically wakes up and gets things moving). It's local with no telemetry. Grateful for the feedback from our users from the first launch. Would be grateful for bug reports, other problems, ideas, questions or suggestions. Thanks, Chris

items.title: Show HN: Vibivibi – End-to-end encrypted sharing of Coding Agent sessions
items.summary: Hi HN, I'm Hongyin. I built Vibivibi ( https://vibivibi.com ) because I kept starting a coding agent session on my laptop and wanting to continue it on a server, or hand it to a colleague. I want an easier way to do it but won’t trust anyone hosting my traces who promises they won’t sell it (market price per coding trace is $50 to $100). What Vibivibi does: a small CLI, `vibi`, finds the sessions your coding agents keep locally (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Pi), encrypts one on your machine and uploads it. On another machine `vibi pull` puts it back where the agent expects it, so `claude --resume <id>` just continues. `vibi push` can also send a session to someone else by email. Our service cannot read session content. Each user has a key pair made on their first machine; the private key reaches the server only wrapped with a key derived from an encryption password that never leaves the user's machines. Every session version is encrypted with its own random key, which is then wrapped for each recipient (X25519, HKDF, AES-256-GCM). The server sees account emails, public keys, machine names, sizes, timestamps, who sent what to whom, and an optional plain-text label. Sending to someone who doesn't have an account yet works too: the sender's client makes a key pair on their behalf, locks it with a random 12-character passphrase, and shows the sender that passphrase to pass on out of band. When the recipient signs up and enrolls a machine, their client unlocks it locally and re-keys the session to their own key. The client is open source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/subconscious-systems/vibi-cli The crypto and the schemas of everything the client sends live in one package, so the claims above can be checked against the code. It ships as a single executable, no Node or npm needed: `curl -fsSL https://vibivibi.com/install.sh | sh`, or build it yourself. The server (Next.js on Vercel, Postgres, blob storage) is not open source. Pricing: free for 200 MB of encrypted storage and unlimited sends; Pro is $8/month for 20 GB; Team is $15/seat with an admin view and a "send only inside the team" policy. Honest limitations: - There is no password recovery. Forget the encryption password and the key, and everything encrypted for it, is gone. I'd like to hear where the threat model falls short, and which agents or workflows you'd want supported next.

items.title: Show HN: Carve – An open-source Mac agent with a choice of models
items.summary: Hi HN, I built and open-sourced Carve to handle repetitive work in windows you already use. Choose the window in any Mac app where you want it to work, press Option-D, and watch it do what you want. For example, in the demo I show an example CRM and Carve entering contact details and drafting a follow up. It also has the ability to annotate and explain items on the screen. This runs with your own API keys, and can even support OpenRouter, though OpenAI is the best tested. Experimental adapters also for Bedrock, Azure. No reason it couldn't expand beyond experimental support to support more local models. I built this because I found that Claude and Codex were rather clunky when using computer use, I like having a sleek window that just pops up and shows me what it's doing. Also it has the 3 similar modes (approve plan, step by step manual approval, or act directly mode). Local currently covers browser actions via vision models, computer use support is required for operating other native mac apps. This is an ongoing area of work. I'm seeing a lot of demand for local model support and building out relevant tooling so wanted to contribute. We're just now at the point where models are getting fast and smart enough to make rapid computer use possible. You can take a look at the benchmarks in the repository, Carve currently can rapidly and cheaply handle explaining, summarizing, basic navigation, and extraction. Complex, long horizon tasks are a work in progress, though I'm seeing promising results. Failures resemble patterns, and you can identify patterns and fix them by running evaluations in batches. I'd love any feedback on how well the tool works, what you tried, and any issues that you found. Thank you!

items.title: Show HN: Browsentic Open-source Claude for Chrome alternative for any agent CLI
items.summary: A personal agent harness lives in your existing browser, connects to your claude-code (or any other major harness codex or cursor-cli...) NOT the SDK API, exposes web-optimized tools to the harness - that's Browsentic. A free, opensource (Apache 2.0) with rich capabilities alternative to Comet, BrowserOS, Browser-use, Claude for Chrome or nanobrowser. The unique architecture of Browsentic makes it different from all other alternatives. It uses a loopback MCP server that spawns claude/codex/OpenCode/Cursor harness in a detached process. You can already guess, it is a bi-directional MCP, you can browse agentic through the browser harness or through any MCP client. Browsentic doesn't require any new browser to install and not limited to chromium, it supports Firefox as well. By default you don't even need CDP to perform core agentic browsing. Capabilities: core accessibilities (50+ compare to nanobrowser only had 20), custom skill, record-replay, schedule-monitoring-notification, resolves captcha autonomously, has it's own memory, voice orb over web-speech API, can sideload custom tools, platform + browser + agent agnostic It is opensource, no API key, no telemetry & local first and actively maintained and yesterday was the first public stable launch (v0.8.0) Currently I'm the only author but every & any contribution or suggestion will be more than welcome :) Source: https://github.com/imshaikot/browsentic Install guide: https://browsentic.com/install Docs: https://browsentic.com/docs Install video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o8t4l9Q9BkE
